opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think speed should be the goal in itself. A lot of people treat the PhD like a race, as if finishing in four years instead of six proves something. What matters is whether you've actually become an independent researcher by the end, someone who can find a problem worth working on, frame it well, and push it through to something real.

That said, I don't think you should drag it out either. There's a trap where people stay because the PhD feels safe. You have a structure, an advisor, a community, and leaving means facing the question of what you actually want to do. If you're staying mainly to avoid that question, it's probably time to go.

The way I think about it is in terms of opportunity cost, especially in a field moving as fast as AI is right now. Every year you spend has to buy you something you couldn't get elsewhere: a skill, a way of thinking, a body of work you're proud of. Once the marginal year stops giving you that, and you could learn more by building something, joining a lab, or starting a company, I think you should be willing to wrap up, even if it's earlier than the "normal" timeline.

So my answer is: finish when you've gotten what the PhD is uniquely good at giving you. For some people that's three years, for some it's six. The number isn't the point. Being honest with yourself about why you're still there is.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think about it as "how fast can I get out." I think the better question is what you're optimizing for, and speed is usually the wrong variable.

When I started, I had this idea that a PhD was a race, that if I could finish in four years instead of six, that was a win. But the degree itself isn't the thing. What you're really building is a body of work, a reputation in a small community, and the ability to pick good problems on your own. Those things don't compress well. You can rush the paperwork, but you can't rush becoming someone whose judgment people trust.

That said, I also don't believe in lingering. There's a point where staying longer stops adding to you and starts costing you, and you usually feel it before you admit it. For me the signal was when the next project started looking like a variation on the last one instead of a step into something new. That's when I knew I should wrap up.

So my rough heuristic is: finish when you've done one piece of work you'd be proud to be known for, and when you can explain, in a few sentences, what you'd do next and why. If you can't answer the second part, you're not done, no matter how many years it's been. And if you can answer it but you're still around, you're probably just comfortable.

One more thing. I'd tell students not to compare timelines across fields or even across labs. A systems PhD and a theory PhD have completely different clocks. The person who finished in three years might have had a project handed to them. The person who took seven might have changed the field. The number tells you almost nothing on its own.

astra-6.text: I think it depends on what you want to get out of the PhD. Finishing quickly can be good, but I wouldn’t make speed the main goal. The question is whether you’ve learned how to identify an interesting problem, work through uncertainty, and do research independently. At the same time, you don’t want to stay forever waiting for one more result or the perfect thesis. I’d work backward from what I want to do next and ask: What do I still need to learn here, and what would I learn better by moving on?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal should be to become an independent researcher, rather than to finish in a particular number of years. You want to learn how to identify a good problem, make progress when the answer isn’t obvious, and explain why your work matters. That takes time, but staying longer doesn’t automatically mean you’re learning more.

So I’d ask: what would another year give me? If there’s a concrete skill I need to develop or a project that could really change my direction, that might be worthwhile. If I’m just waiting to feel completely ready, I’d be inclined to finish. You can keep growing as a researcher after the PhD.
